Eggs of the Red-cheeked cordon-bleu (Uraeginthus bengalus) incubated at a constant temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C] yield hatchlings after an incubation period of 11 days [ab = 11 days], a developmental duration broadly consistent with that of other small estrildid finches. The newly emerged nestlings weigh just 0.84 grams [Ww0 = 0.84 grams], reflecting the species' altricial mode of development, and they undergo a rapid phase of mass increase during the first week post-hatching. At the moment of hatching, the neonatal wet weight is recorded as 0.65 grams [Wwb = 0.65 grams], a figure that underscores the considerable proportion of the egg contents allocated to albumen and shell rather than to the embryo itself. This modest birth mass imposes a heavy parental investment burden, as the clutch must be brooded almost continuously to maintain optimal thermal conditions for the growing chicks. The embryonic period is relatively short compared to larger passerines, and the small initial size of the neonates is typical of species that produce multiple broods within a single breeding season, allowing for rapid population turnover in their sub-Saharan African savanna habitat. The incubation temperature of 34 °C is at the lower end of the range reported for many tropical passerines, suggesting that the eggs may be relatively tolerant of moderate thermal variation during early development.

Under the thermal conditions typical of an actively foraging adult, which average 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the resting metabolic rate of the Red-cheeked cordon-bleu is approximately 29.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = approximately 29.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This basal oxygen consumption value, measured in post-absorptive individuals during their inactive phase, is consistent with allometric predictions for a bird of this small body size and aligns well with the energetic demands of a predominantly granivorous diet. The elevated ambient temperature of 40.2 °C, which is close to the upper critical temperature for many arid-zone finches, likely represents a thermoneutral point at which metabolic heat production is minimized, allowing the bird to conserve energy during the hottest part of the day. This metabolic strategy is particularly advantageous for a species inhabiting dry, open woodlands and scrub where daytime temperatures frequently exceed 35 °C. The relatively low mass-specific metabolic rate suggests that the Red-cheeked cordon-bleu may employ pronounced behavioral thermoregulation, such as gular fluttering and seeking shade, to avoid the high energetic costs associated with evaporative cooling at these temperatures.

Sexual maturity in the Red-cheeked cordon-bleu is attained at 33 days after hatching [tp = 33 days after hatching] under the standard thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a remarkably rapid developmental trajectory that enables the species to commence breeding within its first year of life. Following gonadal activation, the time from birth to the first successful brood is 310 days [tR = 310 days] when birds are exposed to the same high ambient temperature of 40.2 °C, indicating that while puberty arrives early, actual reproductive effort may be delayed until environmental conditions favor nesting and food availability for the altricial young. at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]This delay is ecologically significant, as it allows the young female to accumulate sufficient body reserves and secure a suitable territory before committing to the energetically demanding process of egg formation and nestling provisioning. The pubertal age of 33 days is among the shortest recorded for any estrildid finch and likely reflects an evolutionary response to high adult mortality rates in their seasonally unpredictable environment. The proximate cue for the onset of gonadal recrudescence appears to be photoperiodic, but the precise dietary factors influencing the timing of first reproduction remain poorly understood.

The ultimate adult wet weight shows a clear sexual dimorphism, with females attaining an ultimate wet weight of 10 grams [Wwi = 10 grams], while males are slightly lighter at 9.8 grams [Wwi = 9.8 grams]. This slight but consistent difference in adult body mass likely reflects the greater energetic investment that females make in egg production, including the formation of calcium-rich eggshells and substantial yolk deposits. Under captive conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximum recorded longevity for this species is estimated at 7.5 years [am = 7.5 years], a substantial lifespan for a bird of this diminutive size and considerably longer than the typical field-based estimates from banding studies in their native range. The discrepancy between captive and wild longevity suggests that predation pressure and food scarcity are significant selective forces shaping the life history of this finch in its natural habitat. Fledging, defined as the age at which the chick achieves its first sustained flight, occurs at 18 days after hatching [tx = 18 days after hatching] when measured under the standard thermal condition of 40.2 °C at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

Females of the Red-cheeked cordon-bleu produce one to four eggs per clutch [N_R_i = one to four eggs per clutch], with an average clutch size that fluctuates seasonally in response to rainfall patterns and the consequent abundance of grass seeds. The frequency of reproductive events is approximately three clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately three clutches per year], a pace that enables the species to capitalize on brief windows of food abundance during the wet season in its East African range. The daily reproduction rate implicit in these parameters yields an annual reproductive output of up to 12 eggs per year [Ri = up to 12 eggs per year], reflecting a relatively high annual reproductive output that compensates for the substantial mortality experienced by eggs, nestlings, and fledglings due to predation by snakes, raptors, and small mammals. Brood parasitism by the pin-tailed whydah (Vidua macroura) further reduces the effective reproductive success of this finch, though the cordon-bleu does not exhibit the fine-scale egg discrimination seen in some other estrildid hosts. Remarkably, under the elevated ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximum reproductive rate, as calculated from the upper bounds of both clutch size and clutch frequency, remains constrained by the species' metabolic capacity and the need for biparental care of the altricial young.
